options.text: A model that settles legal disputes
Using a model, given a rubric of criteria, to grade a piece of text and report which criteria are met
Two models debating until one wins
A human judge assisted by autocomplete

questions.explanation: It's a judge with a grading sheet: text in, rubric in, met/not-met per criterion out — the pattern behind this app's playground feedback and countless real-world quality checks. No courtroom (a), no debate (c), no human in the loop for each grade (d).

questions.prompt: Which rubric criterion is well-written for an LLM judge?

options.text: "The prompt names a specific audience for the output"
"The model's answer will probably be good"

questions.explanation: A good criterion is observable — you can point at the words that satisfy it. 'Names a specific audience' is checkable by reading; 'high quality' (a) and 'feels professional' (b) are vibes the judge must guess at, and (d) judges a future output instead of the text in hand.

questions.prompt: In this app's playgrounds, what does the judge actually grade?

options.text: The model's reply to your prompt
Your PROMPT text — the reply is shown as evidence, but the rubric judges what you wrote
Whether you used the suggested wording

questions.explanation: The skill being taught is prompt-writing, and the reply varies run to run even for the same prompt — so your prompt is the stable evidence, and every criterion is checkable from it alone. That's why criteria read like 'the prompt includes...' rather than 'the answer is...' (a).

questions.prompt: A rubric gives 'names the audience' weight 30 and 'sets a length limit' weight 10, with a passing score of 70. What does this tell you?

options.text: The length limit is three times harder to achieve
Naming the audience is the higher priority, and you can miss the length limit and still pass
You must satisfy both criteria to pass
Weights are decorative and don't affect the score

questions.explanation: Weights encode priorities — the core skill weighs most — and the passing score is deliberately set below 100 so missing the lowest-weight criterion isn't fatal (c). Weight measures importance to the grade, not difficulty (a), and your score is literally the sum of the weights you earned (d).

title: Grade sheet in hand
instructions:
You've seen the machinery — now use it deliberately. Below is the EXACT rubric that will grade you (yes, really — this is the real one). Write a prompt asking the model to draft a short announcement for a community library launching a free 'seed library' (borrow vegetable seeds in spring, return saved seeds in autumn). Satisfy every criterion explicitly:

- audience (weight 25): the prompt names a specific audience for the announcement (e.g. local families new to gardening).
- format (weight 25): the prompt specifies the output format AND a length limit (e.g. a friendly noticeboard poster under 120 words with a headline).
- facts (weight 30): the prompt supplies at least three concrete facts the announcement must include (invent them: launch date, how borrowing works, where to sign up).
- self-check (weight 20): the prompt lists its own requirements and asks the model to check the draft against them before finishing.

Passing is 70 — but you have the grade sheet, so aim for 100.

rubric.description: The prompt names a specific audience for the announcement.
The prompt specifies the output format and a length limit.
The prompt supplies at least three concrete facts the announcement must include.
The prompt asks the model to check its draft against the stated requirements before finishing.
